name: extraction-blind-spots
description: Two ways a perfectly ordinary sentence hides a known person from the extractor, labelled as the misses they are. One page, three phrasings of the same question, one of which works.

pages.title: Dana Reed (advisor)
pages.body: Dana Reed advises on pricing and packaging.

turns.text: did dana send the pricing memo?
turns.note: EXPECTED MISS TODAY — proper-case bias. entity-salience.ts documents that it only sees capitalized runs and @handles, so an all-lowercase turn yields ZERO candidates and volunteerContext returns on its first guard. Labelled by what a human wanted, not by what the code does.

turns.text: Did Dana ever hear back on it?
turns.note: EXPECTED MISS TODAY — sentence-opener glue. "Did" is a hard stopword, but it is capitalized at the sentence start and sits directly in front of the name, so the capitalized-run regex swallows both into ONE candidate, "Did Dana". A multi-token run skips the stopword filter by design (multi-token runs are assumed high-signal), and "did dana" matches no alias, title, or slug. The stopword list cannot save a name it never sees alone.

Same person, same intent, phrased so the name stands alone mid-sentence. Resolves on the alias arm at 0.95. The contrast is what makes the two misses above readable as blind spots rather than a broken fixture.
